paragraphs.heading: Swapping one group for another
paragraphs.text: A substitution reaction is a chemical change in which one functional group in a compound is swapped out for a different one. It also goes by the names single displacement or single substitution reaction. Reactions of this kind matter enormously in organic chemistry. Understanding how a reaction type works helps chemists predict its product and tune conditions such as temperature and the choice of solvent.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting the types
paragraphs.text: Organic substitutions are sorted into electrophilic and nucleophilic kinds. The sorting looks at the reagent involved, at whether the reaction passes through a carbocation, a carbanion or a free radical as its reactive intermediate, and at whether the substrate is aliphatic or aromatic.

paragraphs.heading: Chlorine as an example
paragraphs.text: Halogenation is a good example. When chlorine gas (Cl₂) is irradiated, some of its molecules split into pairs of chlorine radicals (Cl•). One radical breaks a C–H bond in CH₄ and takes the hydrogen, making neutral HCl. The other radical bonds with the leftover CH₃• to give CH₃Cl, methyl chloride.

paragraphs.heading: Nucleophiles and leaving groups
paragraphs.text: In nucleophilic substitution, a nucleophile bonds with or attacks an atom carrying a positive or partly positive charge. It pushes out a weaker nucleophile, which becomes the leaving group, and the positive atom left behind is called the electrophile. The whole molecule holding the electrophile and the leaving group is the substrate, written R−LG. The nucleophile's electron pair forms a new bond, the leaving group departs with an electron pair, and the main product is R−Nuc. The nucleophile is usually neutral or negative, while the substrate is typically neutral or positive.

paragraphs.heading: The two-step route, S_N1
paragraphs.text: Nucleophilic substitution runs by one of two mechanisms, named for their rate laws: S_N1 has a first-order rate law and S_N2 a second-order one. S_N1 takes two steps. First the leaving group departs, leaving a carbocation (C⁺); then the nucleophile attaches to it with a covalent sigma bond. If the carbon is chiral, the product can show inversion or retention of configuration, usually both without preference. A carbocation's stability depends on how many carbons are bonded to it, so S_N1 usually happens at atoms with at least two carbons attached.

paragraphs.heading: The one-step route, S_N2
paragraphs.text: S_N2 happens in a single step: the nucleophile arrives at the same moment the leaving group is pushed out. It always inverts the configuration, so a chiral substrate ends up with flipped stereochemistry, an outcome called a Walden inversion. The attack can happen when the backside approach is not blocked by crowding substituents. That is why S_N2 usually takes place at an unhindered primary carbon, while a crowded tertiary carbon reacts by S_N1 instead.

paragraphs.heading: Acyl and aromatic substitution
paragraphs.text: Other forms include nucleophilic acyl substitution and nucleophilic aromatic substitution. In acyl substitution the nucleophile attacks a carbon double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to another oxygen, or to N, S or a halogen; the double bond opens into a single bond, then reforms and kicks out the leaving group. Aromatic substitution happens on compounds whose double bonds are linked in rings. In electrophilic aromatic substitution, an electrophile E⁺ attacks a benzene ring, a carbocation forms, and finally a proton leaves to give a new aromatic compound.
